implementer: generic California city or county building department running a non-automated, checklist-and-plan-review permitting process under Gov. Code 65850.5, plus the investor-owned utility interconnection desk under CPUC Electric Rule 21 (PG&E used as the exemplar tariff)
process: Residential rooftop PV (and paired storage) on the non-automated path: application and completeness screening against a locally adopted checklist, staff plan check across structural, electrical and fire disciplines with correction/resubmittal loops, nondiscretionary permit issuance, a single consolidated final inspection with a re-inspection loop, and the legally separate utility interconnection track ending in a Permission to Operate letter.

denial_rate_note: Structurally near zero and not published anywhere. Gov. Code 65850.5(b) compels administrative approval and limits review to health and safety; a denial requires the building official to make a substantial-evidence finding of specific, adverse impact (A09), then written findings explaining why every feasible mitigation was rejected, where 'feasible method' is statutorily defined to include any mitigation the jurisdiction accepted on a similar prior application. No California source in this corpus reports a residential rooftop solar denial rate.

timing_gold.end_to_end_scope: permit submission -> final passed inspection, business days, traditional (non-automated) permits, 29 AHJs nationally (2024). The directly comparable SolarAPP+ figure is 37 business days, a 12-day or roughly 24% difference at the median.
timing_gold.p90_scope: permit submission -> inspections complete, business days, 0-10 kW PV-only, 2023, national, all paths pooled (SolarTRACE); no traditional-only p90 is published.
timing_gold.end_to_end_to_pto_scope: permit submission -> PTO approved, business days, 0-10 kW PV-only, 2023, national, all paths pooled (SolarTRACE n=56,582).
timing_gold.contract_to_pto_scope: customer contract signing -> PTO granted, business days, California, 0-10 kW PV-only, 2023 (SolarTRACE state-level, n=40,259). National median for the same year is 97. This is the figure that best answers 'how long does rooftop solar take in California', and roughly half of it is pre-submittal design and contractor scheduling that no regulator controls.
timing_gold.source: Performance Review 2024 (S38) for the traditional-vs-SolarAPP+ arms; SolarTRACE 2025-09-09 dataset (S48b) for California state-level medians and national phase quartiles including p90; SolarTRACE retrospective (S43b) for total project time; PG&E Rule 21 tariff and NEM page (S151, S153) as the exemplar interconnection commitment; the Guidebook (S20) for the design targets.
timing_gold.quote: the median duration from permit submission to final passed inspection was 37 business days for all SolarAPP+ permits compared to 49 business days for traditional permits

permit.note: Traditional permit review (submission to issuance) median 7 business days for both PV-only and PV+storage across 33 AHJs in 2024; the pilot-era figure was 9 days. California statewide median was 4 business days in 2023 and 1 in 2024 (SolarTRACE), well below the national traditional median. p90 = 29 business days (SolarTRACE 2023, national). The design target is over-the-counter issuance or a maximum of 1-3 days, so the median runs about 2-7x the Guidebook recommendation and the tail far worse: 12% of traditional permits exceeded 30 business days and 4% exceeded 60. Note that the statute itself sets NO day-count -- the widely cited 'three-day' figure is the Guidebook's recommendation, not law.

inspection.note: Install complete -> last passed inspection: California statewide median 11 business days for 0-10 kW PV-only in 2023 (18 in 2022, 10 in 2024), PV+storage 12; national median also 11, p90 52. The Guidebook expects one or two days from notification. Inspection failure rate for traditional PV-only projects was about 35% in 2024, and Gov. Code 65850.5(h) exempts the subsequent inspection from the timeliness rule, so the rework tail is unregulated.

interconnection.note: Final interconnection request -> PTO granted: national median 10 business days in 2023, p90 48, both far worse than 2022 (median 6, p90 30); California statewide median 12. Tariff ceiling is 'normally not later than thirty (30) Business Days' after the three preconditions, and the exemplar IOU advertises 5-10 business days typical. The SolarTRACE retrospective attributes the 2023 national deterioration primarily to California, i.e. the NEM 2.0 -> NEM 3.0 transition surge.

known_gaps: This model has no single implementer, so it cannot be scored on fee at all. There is no statewide California residential solar permit fee: the Guidebook's model ordinance leaves the fee schedule as a literal placeholder, and observed SolarTRACE medians across just the three AHJs in this corpus span $268.80 to $483.80 for the same 1-10 kW residential permit. A11 therefore carries a null amount by design.

The 'traditional' arm of every NREL/NLR comparison is defined by the AHJs that volunteered data, not by a random sample. The 41 contributing AHJs in the 2024 review had all already adopted SolarAPP+ and supplied their own traditional-permit records for comparison, so they may have had unusually efficient traditional processes to begin with. The Performance Review states plainly that the comparison 'does not control for potentially confounding factors' and that installers self-select between paths.

Permit-review medians silently absorb the resubmittal loop. SolarTRACE counts permits requiring changes and resubmission from the original submittal date, and the Performance Review's traditional figures deliberately 'reflect timelines for a single permit entry' excluding revisions for apples-to-apples comparison. The two observed sources therefore treat A05 and A08 oppositely, and neither isolates rework latency.

No observed source separates the statutory expedited checklist path from ordinary plan review. 'Traditional' in the Performance Review means only 'non-automated'; a jurisdiction's expedited-checklist projects and its full plan-review projects are pooled. The distinction that Gov. Code 65850.5(g) creates is therefore invisible in every timing figure in this model.

Whether a given AHJ holds a fire-authority delegation agreement -- the one lawful exception to the single-inspection guarantee under 65850.5(h) -- is essentially never published. A07 is modelled from the statutory text plus Oakland's staff report describing the negotiation, not from any systematic source.

CPUC Decision D.20-09-035 requires each IOU to report 19 interconnection timeline metrics quarterly, yet the CPUC's own page records that it 'did not mandate reporting for net energy metering (NEM) systems smaller than 30 kVA' -- which the same page says represent the majority of California Rule 21 interconnections. The single richest potential observed dataset on residential PTO timing structurally excludes residential projects.

The Guidebook is the statutorily named playbook and it is stale. The 4th edition dates from Winter 2019 and predates both SolarAPP+ adoption at scale and SB 379 (2022) entirely; no 5th edition incorporating the automated-permitting mandate was located. Gov. Code 65850.5(g)(2) still requires local ordinances to substantially conform to a document that does not mention the state's own later mandate.

SolarTRACE's 2024 columns rest on sharply reduced volumes (1,874 California PV-only installs against 40,259 in 2023) because the dataset was completed 2025-09-09 with partial 2024 coverage. The 2024 improvements in permit and inspection medians should not be read as a trend.

After the SB 379 deadlines this model describes a jurisdiction that is arguably out of compliance for SolarAPP+-eligible systems, since Gov. Code 65850.52(b) requires real-time issuance for systems up to 38.4 kW AC. It remains the correct baseline for ineligible configurations (ground-mounted, ballasted, multi-family, homeowner-installed) and for AHJs that are exempt or non-compliant, but it should not be read as a lawful design for eligible systems post-2023/2024.
notes: Why this model exists and what it is for: it is the counterfactual arm against which both implementer models are scored, built from the statute plus the Guidebook the statute names plus the Performance Review's 'traditional' baselines, with no single jurisdiction's practice standing in for it. Four points a solver must get right. (1) The statute fixes no permit turnaround at all. Gov. Code 65850.5 mandates an 'expedited, streamlined' checklist process and a single consolidated inspection but delegates every day-count to local ordinance and to the Guidebook's recommendation of over-the-counter or a 1-3 day maximum; the commonly cited 'three-day rule' is not statutory text, and only the 2015 ordinance-adoption deadline and SB 379's 2023/2024 platform deadlines are hard dates. (2) The single-inspection guarantee is narrower than it looks: it applies only to expedited-eligible systems, it yields to a separate fire safety inspection where the AHJ lacks a delegation agreement, and 65850.5(h) expressly frees every subsequent inspection from the timeliness rule -- so failing an inspection moves the applicant from a regulated clock onto an unregulated one, which is the structural reason inspection rework dominates the long tail. (3) Approval is nondiscretionary, so the graph has no real decision node on the main path; A09's use-permit referral and A10's appeal are the only discretionary branches and both are deliberately hard to reach. (4) The permitting and interconnection tracks are legally separate under 65850.52(g) and A22 is the seam: because the tariff will not start its 30-business-day PTO clock without the AHJ's final electric inspection clearance, all upstream plan-check and inspection delay passes straight through to the PTO date. The headline contrast with the automated path is 49 versus 37 business days from permit submission to passed inspection, driven almost entirely by the permit-review phase (7 days versus 0), while the inspection and interconnection phases are largely unchanged -- automation moves one phase, not the whole process. gold_tier is 'designed+observed' because the graph is designed-tier while every timing figure is records-derived; per-tier scoring should treat the process model as designed-only. Document ids are the corpus source_ids from corpus/realworld/solar_permit/sources.json.
